title: Julia Child, la Grandes Gourmande
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile Julia Child, the American chef who introduced many Americans to French cooking. Covers her Pasadena birth and upbringing, Smith College, early advertising work, her OSS service in World War II (including the shark repellent project and meeting husband Paul Child), the 1948 meal at La Couronne in Normandy, her Le Cordon Bleu training and the cooking school she co-founded with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle, the cookbook Mastering the Art of French Cooking and editor Judith Jones, her PBS show The French Chef and its legacy, her famous kitchen mistakes, why she was beloved (fresh ingredients, wine, butter, approachability), signature recipes, and her death in 2004 and Neptune Memorial Reef burial. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about episode count and Olympic pools and Big Macs.
topics: Mastering the Art of French Cooking

segments.title: Co-ED sponsor read and intro
segments.summary: Opening banter and a sponsor read for the Cooperative for Education (CoEd), with a Thanksgiving greeting and a call to sponsor Guatemalan students and enter a virtual hangout raffle.

segments.title: Introduction to Julia Child
segments.summary: Hosts introduce Julia Child as a famous cook, joke about Chuck's impression of her, and note she was American, not British, and that she helped introduce America to real food through French cuisine.

segments.title: Early life and Smith College
segments.summary: Julia McWilliams was born in Pasadena to a well-off family; she attended Smith College, was athletic and sociable, graduated in 1934, and worked as an advertising copywriter in New York for Sloan's.

segments.title: OSS service and the shark repellent
segments.summary: During World War II Julia joined the Office of Strategic Services (OSS), doing card-file work and rising in rank; she worked on a shark repellent project that used decayed shark meat, organic acids and copper acetate, and was later chief of the registry and posted to China and Ceylon.

segments.title: Meeting Paul Child and the 1948 lunch at La Couronne
segments.summary: Julia met her future husband Paul Child in the OSS; they married in 1946 and stayed together until his death in 1994. In France in 1948 Paul took her to La Couronne in Normandy, where she had oysters and sole meunière, which she called the most exciting meal of her life.

segments.title: Hosts' tangents on food and Julia's tastes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss French cuisine as humble with quality ingredients, joke about Julia's tastes such as ketchup, frozen peas, and sushi, and reflect on her post-war American food context.

segments.title: Le Cordon Bleu and the cooking school
segments.summary: Julia began cooking classes, enrolled at Le Cordon Bleu in 1951, and that year co-founded L'École des Trois Gourmandes with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle. Chuck notes she was one of very few women in her class and that her kitchen is now in the Smithsonian.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break before the next segment.

segments.title: Mastering the Art of French Cooking and Judith Jones
segments.summary: The hosts describe the cookbook Mastering the Art of French Cooking, which explained techniques and tools for home cooks. It was rejected by several publishers before editor Judith Jones at Alfred A. Knopf took it on; Jones had earlier published The Diary of a Young Girl (Anne Frank).
topics: Mastering the Art of French Cooking

segments.title: Cookbook success and PBS debut
segments.summary: The cookbook became a bestseller and a kitchen bible; volume two came out in 1970. Julia appeared on WGBH's book review show making an omelet, which led to her own show, The French Chef.

segments.title: The French Chef and TV legacy
segments.summary: The French Chef premiered on WGBH within a year and ran for ten years, spreading via PBS and the BBC. Julia won an Emmy and a Peabody and the show featured open captioning. Her closing phrase was bon appetit.

segments.title: Mistakes on camera and the kitchen-home studio
segments.summary: Julia left mistakes in her shows, including the fallen cake, and the dropped turkey legend, which Snopes traced to a potato pancake she flipped and repaired. Her later shows were filmed in her Cambridge home kitchen, designed with Paul's help.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break before the next segment.

segments.title: Why Julia Child was beloved
segments.summary: The hosts explain her appeal: fresh ingredients, letting food taste like itself, normalizing wine (including drinking on camera), her humor, her Letterman appearance, and her Sardines-level approachability with favorite foods like Costco hot dogs and In-N-Out.

segments.title: Butter, moderation, and wine and beer tastes
segments.summary: She championed real butter and cream, the quote about everything in moderation including moderation, and Chuck offers a tip of mixing butter with olive oil. The hosts also mention her Nine-Julia-era drinking habits and the upside-down Martini.

segments.title: Signature recipes
segments.summary: Discussion of her best-known recipes from Mastering the Art of French Cooking: boeuf bourguignon, quiche Lorraine (with blanching bacon), cassoulet, chocolate mousse, and French onion soup, plus a movie reference to Julie and Julia.

segments.title: Death and Neptune Memorial Reef burial
segments.summary: Julia died in August 2004 at age 91 of liver failure at her Montecito home. Her cremated remains were mixed into a headstone placed in the Neptune Memorial Reef off Key Biscayne, Florida, with a knife-and-fork plaque.
